newsitem.title: USA: Stocks drop seen influencing consumers but not much.
newsitem.headline: Stocks drop seen influencing consumers but not much.

text.p: Will consumers close their wallets and spend more cautiously because the stock market has fallen nearly 10 percent since its peak earlier this year?
It's an important question for economists on Wall Street and at the Federal Reserve who try to figure how the economy will look six months down the road.
"The decline could influence consumer sentiment, causing some moderate effect on the downside in consumer spending in the second half," said David Jones of Aubrey G. Lanston and Co.
But opinion varies widely on how much weight to give the "wealth effect." In theory, rising stock market values make consumers feel richer and spend more freely, even if they don't sell their stocks.
Wall Street estimates the stock market since 1994 has added about $3 trillion to total household financial wealth.
Conversely, a falling stock market should make consumers feel poorer and more careful with their money.

With the market erasing the gains made so far this year and beginning to take aim on the 60 percent rise in the Dow Jones Industrial Average that took place in 1995 and 1996, the outlook for consumer spending could be less buoyant.
Economists in the past have talked about the so-called nickel impact, meaning that each increase of $1 in net worth generates 5 cents in additional spending.

But in recent years, the connection has become more tenuous. Although fortunes have been made in the great bull market and luxury items from top of the line autos to yachts to dream vacations are doing well, successful investors are hardly going wild.

Average Amricans have also felt a lift from the runup in stocks through mutual funds and savings programmes at their workplaces. Analysts estimate that some 43 percent of U.S. households hold stocks either outright or in retirement programmes.

But much of this money is esentially untouchable until retirement, so although investors are aware that their nestegg had been growing, they realise their dreams will have to wait and may even be eroded, as is happening now.
Moreover, the baby boom generation, experts say, is socking away money at a fierce pace, worried that Social Security will not be a reliable safety net when they are due to retire.

Even the Federal Reserve, which last month helped puncture the stock market boom with its first interest rate increase in over two years is not certain how the wealth effect plays into the economic tapestry.

"Since we don't know how much of the strong consumption has been attributable to the rise in the stock market, it's hard to predict how much a leveling out will affect it," Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said in an interview on Reuters Financial Television last week.

Many analysts take the view that, at least, the strong market has had a prounounced effect on consumer confidence, although it is difficult to quantify the actual effect at car dealerships and shopping malls.

"My perception is that wealth effect has had a small effect on consumer spending so the declining market will not have a big impact although there could be some effect on consumer confidence," said Elliott Platt of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.

Others argue that the decline in the market will not have any affect on consumer spending in the least, taking the view that that there is a lag time between the increase in stock values and when it begins to show up in overall spending.
"It takes a long time for changes in stock prices to change people's perception of wealth," says Michael Moran of Daiwa Securities Inc.
Adds David Sloan of I.D.E.A, "I don't think we have seen the full impact on consumer spending of past rises in the stock market so any decline will take even longer."
